items.title: Govt scrambles to solve fuel crisis without clear end in sight, divided on fava bean import ban; Quintet tries to balance competing political initiatives; RSF continues Blue Nile push; Military sets sights on Darfur
items.description: Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . The struggling wartime economy took center stage this week in Sudan with a pair of issues at the heart of daily life. The first is a fuel crisis that has grown increasingly worse in recent weeks as gas stations have become makeshift campsites and prices have skyrocketed. While the government has projected an outward image of assurance, behind closed doors, the wheels are turning to try to bring fuel to the nine states under military control. The plan has two axes, sources informed of the discussion told Mada Masr. The first is essentially a triage: tighten fuel allocations and movement to where it is needed. Various government bodies have tried their hand at centralizing authority to better streamline decision-making, but Sudan’s fractured executive apparatus has seen more attempts than results. The second part of the plan would require solving the issue at its source: bringing in new supplies to offset the non-performing domestic oil sector. For this, Transitional Sovereignty Council chair Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is holding talks with Saudi Arabia. But as an informed TSF source told Mada Masr, the government cannot commit to a timeline to end the crisis until external agreements are finalized and the necessary financial guarantees are in place. Alongside the fuel crisis, more potential trouble looms on the horizon, and this one is of the government’s own making. At the beginning of October, the Agriculture Ministry announced it would implement a prime ministerial decree banning fava bean imports in order to bolster domestic production and save foreign currency. In the last two weeks, the move has come in for fierce public criticism, which has been mirrored by criticism from the government and traders, sources in both arenas told Mada Masr. The concern centers on whether a domestic agriculture sector strained by war and the fuel crisis can realistically carry the burden of producing enough supply of the daily food staple. Government sources told Mada Masr that the process in announcing the decision was flawed, and the Cabinet does not have the required data to ensure the ban won’t have disastrous effects. State-level administrative officials and traders chimed in to argue that the timing of the decision hasn’t given farmers enough time to adjust this season’s production plan to bolster supply. While a source in Prime Minister Kamel Idris’s office projected confidence that the Agriculture Ministry has the necessary data to back up the soundness of the ban, a source in the ministry said that officials are already discussing contingency plans. The political front this week saw yet another spin on the merry-go-round of political initiatives. The Quintet — which comprises the African Union, the United Nations, the Arab League, the European Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development — is trying to carefully engage with all competing political initiatives without endorsing any. This comes amid increasing divides between civilian political groups and the preparatory committee leading the government-sponsored internal dialogue over who gets to set its terms and who gets to participate. Both sides of the divide are trying to influence the AU to gain a leg up. On the military front, the Rapid Support Forces continued this week to push for greater control of the Blue Nile locality of Wad al-Mahi. The military was able to push the advance back in a counteroffensive on October 9. On the western front, the military launched airstrikes on RSF positions as it looked to translate its control of North Kordofan into a stronger position in West Kordofan to take the strategic city of Nuhud. Control of Nuhud would open the door to North Darfur, on which they already have their sights set, military sources told Mada Masr. From within Darfur, the military made strategic gains this week, with the joint forces advancing from their remaining garrisons in the north of the region down into West Darfur, where they seized control of the agriculturally rich area of Bir Keleikil. *** Burhan takes direct control of oil file amid worsening fuel shortages Crowded gas station in Khartoum, September 27. Courtesy: Nepta Petroleum CO.LTD via Facebook. The Sudanese government is scrambling for solutions in the face of a worsening fuel crisis marked by long lines at filling stations and growing concerns over everything from trade to markets to the ongoing planting season. Across the nine states under military control, gas stations have effectively turned into makeshift campsites. People wait for one or two days at a time just to secure a single liter of gasoline or diesel — fuel that now costs around 47,000 Sudanese pounds per liter or as high as 80,000 pounds on the black market. This crisis has driven up food prices and now threatens the summer harvest season. Thousands of farmers are left waiting for fuel to harvest their crops, while the failure of the winter planting season also looms on the horizon. The state has not admitted outright that there is a fuel crisis, only vaguely acknowledging it to reassure citizens that everything is all right. However, the flurry of meetings and statements of reassurance are enough to show the frenetic pace of what is happening behind the scenes. And indeed, officials across different levels of government who spoke to Mada Masr talked about a crisis management plan that has taken different directions in recent weeks. But across all levels, the infighting that has plagued the government in a host of other policy issues has derailed any potential momentum in what is already a steep climb out of a crisis caused by an oil sector that has been brought to halt by the war and a lack of foreign currency. Now, Burhan is trying to transcend weeks of missteps by taking direct control of the file, making oil procurement the purview of a revived government body under his control and trying to secure a lifeline from Saudi Arabia. But neither of these moves have borne fruit as of yet, and, thus, there is no timeline for the end of the crisis. The government cannot commit to a timeline until external agreements are finalized and the necessary financial guarantees are in place, a TSC source told Mada Masr. Its immediate aim is to secure regular supplies for the capital and the states, including the agricultural and service sectors, instead of relying on occasional shipments to keep shortages at bay. The root of the oil crisis lies in the fact that the war has forced oil fields out of service, leaving Sudan increasingly reliant on imported fuel and putting further strain on its already depleted foreign currency reserves, a senior Energy Ministry official told Mada Masr. The ministry has been working with the Central Bank of Sudan and other authorities to tackle logistical obstacles, manage strategic reserves and distribute available supplies among the states. Yet the bottlenecks remain, despite the measures taken so far and the TSC’s decision to intervene directly, the official said. On September 20, the TSC assigned its member, Shams Eddin Kabbashi, to oversee the oil portfolio, in a bid to contain the crisis by tightening coordination between the institutions responsible for imports, financing and supply, the TSC source told Mada Masr. Kabbashi’s mandate extends to oil contracts, financing mechanisms and the restructuring of institutions in the sector, particularly the Sudanese Petroleum Corporation, the state-owned company dissolved in 2019 before the fall of former President Omar al-Bashir. The stated aim is to bring sovereign and executive institutions under a more coordinated oversight system, allowing decisions on imports and financing to be tracked directly, the source said. But elevating the portfolio to the sovereign level has not resolved the underlying problems. By the time Kabbashi was brought in, financing difficulties had already mounted, and foreign contracts had been delayed. Importing companies were also struggling to secure the required volumes due to difficulties obtaining foreign currency and bank guarantees, the source explained. His appointment was supposed to address these failures and align the decisions of the Energy Ministry, the Central Bank of Sudan and financial authorities. So far, however, the response has remained largely procedural — reorganizing import mechanisms and negotiating with suppliers. Until financing and shipping arrangements are completed, new contracts cannot deliver the supplies the market needs, the source said. Faced with this lack of motion, the Energy Ministry officials and Idris made renewed efforts earlier this month. On October 9, Energy Minister Moatasim Ibrahim Ahmed announced additional fuel supplies for production and service sectors at a meeting chaired by Idris. Officials also approved a plan to tackle import challenges and ensure a regular supply flow. The meeting brought together the ministry’s undersecretary, the central bank’s first deputy governor and the General Intelligence Service’s Economic Security Department head. But the announcement offered little indication of what the plan would deliver in practice. No figures were provided for the additional volumes, their distribution across the country or when they would reach the market. As the government struggles to ease fuel shortages, 24 importing companies have challenged the rules governing who gets to bring supplies into the country. In a joint memorandum submitted to Burhan on October 6, the companies warned that distortions of competition in the petroleum products market threaten supply and price stability, a source at one of the companies that signed the memo told Mada Masr. Their complaints focus on barriers to market entry: the 200 kilogram gold deposit now required by the central bank for each shipment as collateral and the financing arrangements imposed on overseas purchases, he added. The companies see the rules as favoring a small group of importers, leaving others unable to meet the requirements and compete on equal terms. They are asking to finance imports using their own resources and other legitimate sources, rather than being restricted to designated channels for obtaining foreign currency, the source said. Greater flexibility, the source explained, would ease pressure on the central bank’s reserves and bring more importers into a market struggling to secure enough fuel. The source added that the companies are also demanding a transparent system for allocating import quotas, with publicly announced volumes distributed according to uniform criteria. Clear allocations would allow companies to negotiate contracts and secure financing with greater certainty, while giving regulators a way to monitor contracted quantities, incoming shipments and distribution. To review the rules, the memorandum proposes a TSC committee comprising the central bank, relevant ministries and government agencies and representatives of import and distribution companies, the source said. But rather than empower private sector actors to succeed where the state has so far failed, Khartoum has been pursuing greater control over fuel imports. In June, the Cabinet decided that the state would import petroleum products directly, tasking the finance and energy ministries, the central bank and the Economic Security Department with carrying out the plan. The move was intended to secure supplies, stabilize the market and ease pressure on the exchange rate. A Cabinet official told Mada Masr that it is not meant to displace private importers but to give the state greater scope to intervene when necessary. But adding the state to the pool of importers does not fix the problems that have constrained them all: access to foreign currency and bank guarantees and the timely arrival of shipments. Against this backdrop, the presidency is moving to centralize oversight of the sector through a proposed “supreme oil council” chaired by Burhan and comprising the prime minister, the energy minister and the central bank governor, a second TSC source told Mada Masr. The council’s formation is nearing completion, the source said. It would set strategic priorities and oversee decisions on securing petroleum products in coordination with the Cabinet, while executive agencies would retain responsibility for technical and operational matters under the powers defined in official decrees, he added. The proposed council would expand sovereign oversight of a sector where economic policymaking, commercial contracts, bank financing and economic security intersect. But it also raises questions about who would ultimately be in charge and how the new body would divide responsibilities with the prime minister’s office and the Energy Ministry, particularly given Kabbashi’s existing mandate to oversee the oil portfolio. The final division of powers remains unclear, as does whether the council would stick to setting strategic priorities or directly oversee contracts and financing. Meanwhile, the government is trying to bring the Sudanese Petroleum Corporation back into the picture. The state-owned company was dissolved in 2019, with its functions transferred to the Cabinet body responsible for oil and gas, which is now the Energy and Petroleum Ministry. The ministry is working to finalize the corporation’s legal and administrative framework and determine how it would operate alongside the Cabinet and private importers, a source in the Energy Ministry told Mada Masr. Under the proposed arrangement, the corporation would help expand direct imports, oversee contracts and coordinate supply allocations, though its precise powers and the timing of its return remain unsettled. Whether reviving the corporation will establish a sustainable mechanism for importing and distributing fuel, rather than simply reshuffle responsibilities among government institutions, remains to be seen. But its role could prove important if the government succeeds in securing a supply agreement with Saudi Aramco, one of the main avenues it is currently pursuing to ease the shortages. Talks with the Saudi state-owned energy giant began in 2024 but stalled before resuming earlier this year. They have now reached an advanced stage, with a target for an agreement to be finalized before the end of 2026, the Energy Ministry source said. The proposed deal would require bank guarantees from the Central Bank of Sudan and other financial authorities. According to the source, a specialized Sudanese entity, likely the Sudanese Petroleum Corporation in coordination with the ministry, would sign the contract and manage deliveries under terms covering quantities, scheduling, financing and payment that are still being negotiated. An agreement could offer a more reliable way to secure part of Sudan’s fuel needs than the piecemeal imports that have left supplies exposed to financing problems and delays. But the negotiations have yet to produce a signed contract, let alone publicly disclosed quantities, costs or payment terms. And a penned deal would still leave the government with the challenge of securing guarantees, meeting its financial commitments and getting the fuel shipped, offloaded and distributed across the country, the source added. Saudi Arabia’s recent involvement in Sudan’s oil sector is not limited to the Aramco talks. On September 10, Sudan signed a memorandum of understanding with Saudi Twaik Group to rehabilitate the Jaili oil refinery, which was forced out of service during the first months of the war, and build a new one in Port Sudan. The projects point to an effort to rebuild Sudan’s battered oil infrastructure, but, for now, they remain at the memorandum stage, with a final agreement and implementation still to come. The Aramco talks and the refinery memorandum came up again on Thursday in Riyadh. Sudan’s energy minister met with the Saudi assistant energy minister on the sidelines of the International Energy Forum and the World Petroleum Congress, where they discussed avenues to strengthen bilateral strategic cooperation on oil, gas and electricity as well as current arrangements, according to a statement from Sudan’s ministry. *** Fava bean import ban proceeds without cross-ministry review, raises supply concerns Fava bean agriculture in Sudan. Courtesy: Al Ula Press Despite this fuel crisis that is squeezing farmers and raising the cost of agricultural production, the Sudanese government announced in early October that it was moving forward with a long-postponed ban on the import of fava beans, a staple food consumed daily by millions of Sudanese. The ban was announced by the Agriculture Ministry on October 2 in a decision that saw it withdraw the issuance of no-objection certificates for fava bean imports from any country. The move was announced as implementing an order issued by Idris in April, which his office presented as giving local producers a boost while conserving foreign currency. But in the two weeks that have followed the announcement, public, governmental and agricultural and trade sector criticism has pushed back on whether the country is ready for such a move, with many saying it could have negative effects on the availability and price of a vital, daily food. Despite the criticism, the ban remains in effect. But there are signs of concern over the blowback from the decision. Agriculture Minister Essmat Qurashy has tried to distance himself from the decision after it drew public criticism. At a conference on October 7, he said the decision fell under the Trade Ministry’s jurisdiction and that his ministry only suspended the certificates in line with an earlier ban. A senior official at Idris’s office told Mada Masr that the government remains confident in the decision. Agriculture Ministry estimates show good stocks and a harvest expected to cover market demand, the official told Mada Masr. But the ministry itself is less confident. Officials are now discussing contingency measures for supply disruptions that could arise while the ban remains in force, an Agriculture Ministry official told Mada Masr. These include a joint review of stocks and consumption by the agriculture, finance and trade ministries; a review of shipments covered by contracts signed before the ban; and transitional arrangements to prevent an abrupt drop in supply. Officials are also considering fixed import quotas if a supply gap is confirmed. The aim would be to allow imports when necessary while preserving protections for domestic farmers, the official said. The official did not say whether the proposals have been formalized or when a decision might be made — leaving the government still weighing how to respond if the supply problems the measures are meant to prevent materialize. Preventing the import of fava beans was first proposed by the Agriculture Ministry in late 2025 to encourage the crop’s cultivation alongside wheat, but its implementation was postponed until domestic production was sufficient to support the country’s demands, a Finance Ministry source told Mada Masr. That sense changed as millions of Sudanese returned to areas under military control, increasing demand for imported goods to meet their needs. According to the Finance Ministry source, Idris ordered the ban to be implemented in mid-September. Qurashy then followed suit with the early October decision. For the Finance Ministry source, the way the ban was rolled out is itself a concern, raising serious reservations within the ministry. A measure affecting a food staple for millions should be preceded by a joint review of production, trade and financial data, the official said, to allow the government to assess the supply and price risks before shutting off imports. No transition period was allotted for importers to settle commitments or for officials to establish whether available stocks could cover demand, he added. To determine the right time for the ban to be imposed, economic authorities need reliable figures on current inventories, the coming harvest and consumption across Sudan’s states — data they do not have, the source said. Without this data, authorities risk discovering a supply gap only after it begins to push prices up. That would place an extra burden on low-income households already struggling with rising food, transport and basic service costs, the official added. The source in Idris’s office defended the ban as part of a wider push to boost domestic production and reduce reliance on imported agricultural goods. Cheap imports, he argued, leave local farmers struggling to sell their crops at prices that cover cultivation costs, particularly as fuel, fertilizer, labor and other expenses keep rising. The market, however, needs supplies throughout the year, not just a harvest deemed sufficient. Domestic availability depends on harvest schedules and traders’ capacity to store and transport crops, leaving imports to fill gaps when supplies in wholesale markets fall or prices rise, an import-export company source told Mada Masr. The risks may emerge gradually as traders’ stocks dwindle and replacement supplies fail to arrive in time, the source warned. Prices could start rising even before a shortage materializes, as expectations of tighter supply feed into the market. Consumers may then turn to other legumes and food products, pushing up demand for substitutes and extending price pressures beyond fava beans themselves, he added. The ban decision also assumes farmers can in fact ramp up production. In Northern State, one of Sudan’s main fava bean-producing regions, farmers are already grappling with rising cultivation costs and limited access to financing, a state executive official told Mada Masr. Higher input costs are forcing farmers to weigh how much land they can afford to plant, particularly when financing is scarce or seeds, fertilizers and other supplies arrive late. Those constraints need to be addressed before the growing season begins if production is to expand, the official said. But that opportunity has already passed for the current season, which began in October, leaving little immediate room for a quick output increase. Costs also do not end with the harvest, he added. Packaging, storing and transporting crops all eat into farmers’ returns, with higher fuel prices, service fees and inter-state transport costs adding to the burden. The result is a widening gap between prices farmers sell at and what consumers in cities actually pay, the official said. The import ban could create room for domestic producers, but only if the government can bring down cultivation and marketing costs and ensure crops reach markets consistently, he added. Imports account for an estimated 15-18 percent of Sudan’s fava bean supply, with the last year sitting at the upper end of that range, according to estimates provided by the Agriculture Ministry official. That may be a relatively small portion of the market, but imports still help fill gaps when domestic stocks run low before the next harvest, said Al-Awad al-Safy, a crop trader in Northern State. Banning them could shift demand toward locally grown beans and improve farmers’ returns, but it could just as easily push prices higher if domestic supplies fall short or production and transportation costs remain high, Safy said. *** Quintet engages Sudan’s rival political initiatives As rival efforts vie to set the terms for Sudan’s political future, the Quintet, the international mediation group on Sudan, is trying to engage competing Sudanese camps without throwing its weight behind any one initiative. The group, which comprises the African Union, the United Nations, the Arab League, the European Union and the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, is consulting forces with “divergent positions on the existing authorities” as it engages with the dialogue backed by Burhan, an AU official told Mada Masr. The aim, the official said, is to coordinate the various initiatives, not to endorse one or settle on a single design for the political process. The Quintet met on Monday with a delegation from the Declaration of Principles Forces — the emerging anti-war alliance trying to establish itself as a new center of political gravity — at the AU headquarters in Addis Ababa. The meeting followed talks in Khartoum last month between the Quintet and the preparatory committee for the internal dialogue. The committee is pursuing its own regional outreach. On Tuesday, it received an invitation from Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the AU’s rotating chair, to visit Burundi in what it aims to be consultations on launching the dialogue. But attempts to coordinate between the initiatives will not, by itself, resolve the dispute over their underlying political terms. While Burhan’s dialogue is being organized under the military-led authorities, the Declaration of Principles Forces is calling for civilian forces to set the political framework, with military actors confined to security and humanitarian matters, a political source who took part in the delegation said. The alliance, which brings together civilian and armed groups led by Abdel Wahid Nur’s Sudan Liberation Movement and includes the opposition Sumud coalition led by former Prime Minister Abdalla Hamdok, laid out its proposal during Monday’s meeting, the political source told Mada Masr. Hamdok attended alongside representatives of the Popular Congress Party, women and youth networks, civil society organizations and independent figures. The proposal links a ceasefire and humanitarian relief to political talks on governance and the reconstruction of state institutions, but the delegation made it clear that military actors should stay out of the political process, the source said. The delegation also wants the National Congress Party, the Islamic current and affiliated groups excluded from the next phase. That demand stems from the alliance’s view that Sudan’s current crisis is rooted in the struggle over power following Bashir’s fall, the source said. Allowing forces linked to the former regime back into the process, the delegation argued, would provoke opposition from revolutionary forces and threaten the durability of any political settlement. The alliance is also tying political negotiations to a tougher approach on arm supplies. During the meeting, it backed the United States-led proposal to extend the UN arms embargo beyond Darfur to cover all of Sudan, arguing that continued weapon shipments and funding to the warring parties would make a lasting ceasefire difficult to secure. The delegation called on the Quintet to work with international sanction bodies to explore ways to curb the flow of arms into the country, the source said. The proposal is already facing opposition at the UN Security Council, where the US draft resolution to expand the embargo has struggled to advance amid resistance from Russia, China and African members of the council. Sudan’s military-led authorities have also staunchly rejected the move, arguing that it would equate the state’s armed forces with a “rebel militia.” While the Quintet is trying to bring Sudan’s competing political camps closer together and establish a common ground for an organized process, it has no authority over matters such as the embargo, the AU official said, commenting on the delegation’s proposal. That alone is enough of a challenge for the mediation body, which has for months failed to move the parties toward an internationally backed political track. The Quintet’s stated position is that any process must be Sudanese-led and Sudanese-owned, preserve the country’s unity and sovereignty and rule out parallel governing structures. In practice, however, that means engaging with forces that reject the dialogue backed by the authorities in Khartoum while trying to coordinate with those same authorities and, at the same time, advance an alternative process under international and regional auspices, the AU official said. The problem of competing initiatives was central to the delegation’s discussions in Addis Ababa. Building on the Quintet’s September meeting with the US-led Quad on Sudan — comprising Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Egypt — on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, the delegation called for a coordinating framework bringing together the Quintet, the Quad and the Troika, made up of the US, the United Kingdom and Norway. Without a common framework, the delegation argued, the proliferation of initiatives has allowed political and military forces to engage with different tracks without a clear understanding of how they fit together, the political source who participated in the delegation said. Yet Sumud itself is now working to establish another political track. A senior member of the coalition’s executive office told Mada Masr that Sumud is moving toward boycotting the internal dialogue, including by staying out of its preparatory committee and any meetings that emerge from it. Instead, Sumud is engaging with civilian forces and regional and international actors to “develop an alternative political track grounded in an agreement among Sudanese forces on the principles of the transitional process and linked to humanitarian and security measures to end the war,” he said. The coalition wants to bring together forces opposed to the internal dialogue and present a common political vision, with civilian forces taking the lead in setting the process’s terms rather than joining one whose political and organizational framework has already been established, the source added. The coalition, the source said, rejects how the committee has been framing itself as “a purely administrative body responsible for organizing meetings” — a position it has advanced in outreach to civilian forces as it tries to secure enough participation to launch the process. The committee has insisted that it does not determine participation criteria, set the political agenda or dictate the dialogue’s outcomes. Civilian forces opposed to the initiative fear that joining a committee formed by the existing authorities would lock them into arrangements that would be difficult to change later, confining their objections to the details of the dialogue rather than allowing them to challenge its underlying framework, the senior Sumud source said. For Sumud, outside backing for the internal dialogue makes no difference and cannot compensate for those structural objections, he added. The preparatory committee had hoped that its meeting with the Quintet last month would help it secure participation from forces still wary of the initiative, a committee source previously told Mada Masr. Now, it is looking to the AU’s current leadership for help. The committee is preparing to visit Burundi for talks with President Evariste Ndayishimiye, the AU’s rotating chair, on arrangements for launching the dialogue, a committee member told Mada Masr. Burundi’s ambassador to Sudan delivered the invitation during a meeting with the committee in Khartoum on Tuesday, the member said. Talks are expected to cover the steps needed to launch the dialogue, the reasons some political forces remain reluctant to participate and how African institutions could help widen participation and support the process. The member said the committee wants to establish a clearer role for the AU in the coming period, particularly in providing “political guarantees” and persuading skeptical forces to join the preparatory consultations. But it also wants to maintain the principle that Sudanese parties should set the agenda and determine the outcomes of their own political process, the member stressed. The initiative rests on the principle that Sudanese should manage the dialogue themselves, with regional and international actors helping to create the conditions for it to proceed. But with the political framework still contested, it is counting on support from Burundi’s presidency to help address concerns that have kept some forces away. It will continue domestic consultations while preparing for the visit, the member added. An African diplomatic source informed of the Burundian presidency’s engagement on Sudan told Mada Masr that the invitation is part of an effort to expand contact with the parties involved in the political process. Burundi’s presidency hopes to encourage initiatives that narrow differences and help create conditions for ending the war, the source said. That outreach, however, should not be mistaken for an endorsement of the committee’s initiative, the source stressed. Like the Quintet, the AU is seeking to engage Sudanese political efforts without appearing to privilege one over the others. The diplomatic source said the invitation does not confer an exclusive mandate on the preparatory committee to manage the political process. AU support will instead depend on whether an initiative can bring more forces into the process and offer political guarantees they can accept, the source added. The AU faces a balancing act of supporting Sudanese ownership of the political process while coordinating domestic initiatives with the Quintet’s efforts, without allowing them to harden into competing tracks that may prove difficult to reconcile later, the source said. *** RSF attempts further push in Blue Nile’s Wad al-Mahi, military repels attack A week after capturing the Kadalo mountains area of the Wad al-Mahi locality in eastern Blue Nile near the Ethiopian border, the RSF attempted to advance further, attacking a new area in the same locality. The military, backed by local civilians, repelled the attack. Both sides subsequently began reinforcing their positions ahead of further operations, according to three military sources. The RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, launched an assault on the Um Darfa town in the early hours of October 9, one of the sources told Mada Masr. The military, supported by Sudan Popular Resistance forces, launched a counteroffensive, repelling the assault and inflicting heavy losses in personnel and equipment, the source said. Residents joined the fighting, taking up light weapons to defend their town alongside the military, an activist in Damazin, the state capital, told Mada Masr. Their involvement played a significant role in repelling the attack, he added. But the fighting has continued beyond the frontlines. The RSF has since continued to target the area with drones, the activist said, including a Sunday strike on the main hospital that injured two medical workers and damaged parts of the facility, forcing it out of service. On Monday, the military said that it shot down a strategic drone near Wad al-Mahi, saying it had tracked the aircraft crossing into Sudan from Ethiopia. The military began reinforcing its positions in eastern Blue Nile the day after the attack on Um Darfa, dispatching dozens of combat vehicles carrying reserve troops to the region’s eastern fronts on October 10, the military source told Mada Masr. The reinforcements, equipped with jamming devices and air defense systems, are intended to secure military-held positions and support operations to retake sites captured by the RSF and are also tasked with clearing key positions along the Ethiopian border, the source added. By Monday, signs of a parallel buildup had emerged across the border. Two military sources told Mada Masr that 40 combat vehicles and dozens of motorcycles had moved from Asosa, in Ethiopia’s Benishangul-Gumuz region, toward Mankush, near the Sudanese border opposite Wad al-Mahi. The sources said the movements could signal preparations for attacks on Abu Gaddaf and Balgwa in the locality, adding that the military had detected them and drawn up plans to counter them. In the Kurmuk locality, where the RSF deployed additional forces last week, 300 RSF fighters and 50 vehicles also launched an attack on October 9 on Jabal Kadam, to the east of the RSF-held Kurmuk city, one of the military sources said. The military managed to draw the attackers into an ambush and repelled the assault, he added. Damazin’s Fourth Infantry Division said the military’s forces inflicted heavy losses on the RSF in personnel and equipment. *** Military steps up air campaign in Kordofan as forces prepare for Darfur fighting As the military presses to consolidate control over North Kordofan and advance into West Kordofan, it stepped up airstrikes on RSF positions across the two states. To push back the military advance, the RSF has repositioned fighters around the strategic city of Nuhud ahead of a possible military push. The military is now reading its divisions as it looks to take the next phase of fighting to Darfur. North Kordofan’s Abu Haraz and West Kordofan’s Um Samima, Khawi, Zeleita and Sarif Ankoush came under airstrikes on Wednesday, a military field source told Mada Masr. The raids killed a number of RSF fighters and destroyed 15 combat vehicles, the source added, describing the current operation as an effort to advance toward the edges of Darfur. The RSF, meanwhile, has moved large numbers of fighters to Nuhud, stationing them along the city’s southern and western outskirts in anticipation of possible surprise attacks, the source said. Nuhud is the northeastern point in West Kordofan’s strategic triangle, alongside Babanusa and Heglig. Whoever controls the city holds a key staging point linking West Kordofan to North Darfur. A retired military officer said the RSF may now prioritize fortifying its positions and troops in Darfur over mounting a sustained resistance in West Kordofan, especially that the military has dismantled its core forces in North Kordofan. The anticipated push westward is also bringing the Sixth Infantry Division back into the Darfur theater. The division endured 18 months of RSF siege in Fasher before the city and its garrison fell in late 2025. It has now been moved from its temporary base in Merowe in Northern State to Khartoum ahead of a redeployment to fight in Darfur. At a farewell ceremony for the division on Tuesday, the Merowe air base commander told troops they would meet again in Fasher. Deputy division commander Abdel Jabbar Babiker said the force is now heading to the frontlines to retake the city. A military source told Mada Masr that the division’s troops had undergone intensive training in preparation for deployment. Forces from the 20th Infantry Division in Daein, the 15th in Zalingei and the 22nd in Babanusa have also been repositioned to join the frontlines, the source added. *** Military repels attack on its positions in South Kordofan’s eastern Nuba Mountains Fighting broke out in Um Deheilib in the eastern Nuba Mountains of South Kordofan on Sunday, when the RSF and its ally, SPLM-N, attacked military positions in the area, a field source among civilians mobilized to fight alongside the military told Mada Masr. Clashes lasted around six hours before the military ultimately repelled the assault, leaving dozens of RSF and allied fighters killed or wounded, the source said. The military also suffered several casualties, he added. The RSF and its allies are seeking to open a new front in the eastern Nuba Mountains, the source said, noting that the military’s 10th Infantry Division in Um Jubeiha has deployed additional troop and logistical reinforcements in preparation. The same day, SPLM-N artillery fire struck Kadugli, the state capital, killing a mother and her three children, the Sudan Doctors Network said . *** Military, allies advance in West Darfur’s border areas Advancing from their strongholds in North Darfur, the military and its allies captured more ground in West Darfur’s border areas this week. Military troops and fighters from the joint force of allied armed movements set out from Gargira in North Darfur on Wednesday and crossed into West Darfur, reaching Bir Keleikil, where they clashed with the RSF for five hours, a field source with the joint force told Mada Masr. The forces ultimately took control of the area, inflicting casualties on the RSF and seizing several combat vehicles, the source added. Joint force fighters posted videos showing the takeover. Bir Keleikil lies around 32 km from the Chadian border, in the eastern part of the Jabal Moon locality. One of West Darfur’s most fertile agricultural areas, it also draws herders during periods of drought. Khartoum-appointed West Darfur Governor Bahr Eddin Karama hailed the recapture in a statement on Wednesday. *** Subscribe to our Lens on Sudan newsletter here . The post Govt scrambles to solve fuel crisis without clear end in sight, divided on fava bean import ban; Quintet tries to balance competing political initiatives; RSF continues Blue Nile push; Military sets sights on Darfur first appeared on Mada Masr .

items.title: Shaheen Afridi wants unity to be Pakistan's identity under his leadership
items.description: Shaheen Shah Afridi has been one of the casualties of Pakistan cricket’s brutal game of captaincy musical chairs. But at a stage in his career when he has much to prove, the left-arm pace spearhead has the One-day International (ODI) captaincy firmly in his grasp, with the 2027 World Cup looming on the horizon. Unlike in 2024, when he was removed as Pakistan’s T20 captain after just one series in charge, the country’s cricket board appears to have committed to giving Shaheen a longer run as leader. Appointed to the ODI role 12 months ago, he is expected to lead Pakistan through to next year’s World Cup in South Africa. When Pakistan take on Sri Lanka in the opening match of the ODI tri-series on Sunday, Shaheen will have Babar Azam among his charges. Babar replaced him as T20 captain in 2024 before eventually making way for Salman Ali Agha. Shaheen, meanwhile, took over the ODI captaincy from former skipper Mohammad Rizwan, who is currently under investigation by the country’s cybercrime agency. Not long ago, Babar, Shaheen and Rizwan formed the core of Pakistan’s leadership group, with Babar shouldering much of the responsibility. He appeared to enjoy the backing of the other two, but the dynamics eventually changed amid a succession of captaincy reshuffles. Despite that turbulent history, Shaheen wants his side to be seen as a united team, with a common objective: winning the 2027 World Cup. “We are united as a team and our collective focus is towards winning the World Cup and how we can do it,” he told reporters at a pre-series press conference at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on Saturday. “The messaging from you [the media] should be good as well, to tell the people that this team is united, there is love in this team and this team tries to play good cricket. “It is just a game. If you portray it to the people, kids in a way that is too serious, they will be worried about why we are not winning.” Shaheen was particularly emphatic in his support for Babar, describing the former captain as the “backbone” of the side. “There is no pressure on Babar, he is our main player,” said the 26-year-old. “He is the backbone of this team. “He has performed well over the past few home series.” Under Shaheen, Pakistan’s ODI side has spent the past year rebuilding, winning all their home series in the process. Those assignments were played on slower surfaces, with spin-friendly pitches used most recently during the series against Australia in May and June. The conditions for the tri-series, however, are expected to offer a different challenge, with pitches being prepared to better resemble those in South Africa. The surfaces appeared greener during Pakistan’s recent T20I series against Sri Lanka, and Shaheen confirmed that there had been a deliberate effort to encourage lateral movement and bounce. “Over the course of the last four one-day series, we have tried to build this team, since our focus is on [next year’s] World Cup and how we can prepare for it,” he said. “Henceforth we have also tried to prepare the wickets accordingly.” Pakistan will also play a five-match ODI series in England before beginning their World Cup campaign against Afghanistan on Oct 8. “We want our fast bowlers to get help [off the surface] so when we play in South Africa and in England, both our bowling and our batting has the potential to get the other team out and chase the runs [respectively],” Shaheen said. The conditions will also influence Pakistan’s team combination, with Shaheen indicating that the side could field three or four fast bowlers. That would make opener-turned-all-rounder Saim Ayub’s contribution with the ball particularly important, despite his recent struggles in T20 and Test cricket. “Saim Ayub may have struggled in T20 cricket, he struggled in the Test match as well,” Shaheen said. “But as far as one-day cricket is concerned, we really need him. “Because if we go with three or four pacers, then the team needs his bowling. If we keep giving him opportunities, he will thrive for Pakistan.” Brook, Mendis look ahead to Tri-Series England and Sri Lanka captains, Harry Brook and Kusal Mendis are also looking forward to the challenge of the tri-series. “I think it’s a great opportunity to play a tri series in Pakistan against two very strong sides. I think it will definitely hold us in good stead knowing that there is a final at the end of the series as well,” said Brook in the captains’ press conference. “Pakistan is a great place to play cricket as well and we know how passionate the crowd can be.” He added that the tri-series will allow the side to assess where they stand in ODIs, after a successful few months during which the team has bonded and gotten a real sense of what they want to achieve on the field. “We wanna be a side where we can win in any conditions against any opposition, “Pakistan are gonna present us with challenges we probably haven’t quite faced yet as an ODI side, and we’re really looking forward to the opportunity of playing Pakistan and Sri Lanka in subcontinental conditions,” he said. Kusal Mendis also said the series will be important for all teams, adding that the Sri Lankan side had trained for a few days following the conclusion of the T20I series. The series had ended in a 2-1 win for Pakistan, but Sri Lanka had clinched the third fixture by a convincing eight wickets, allowing them to enter the ODI series on a high. “[In the] last game, the bowling part was done really well, and myself and Kamindu batted really well,” he said, adding that finishing on a “positive” note allowed the side to enter this tri-series with confidence and the knowledge that they “know how to play.” “We have very good, talented senior players, a couple of all-rounders, and we played really well in the England series also,” he said, referring to the side’s white-ball tour of England where the ODI series had ended in a 2-1 win for the hosts. “I hope we can do well in this tournament.” “I have no doubt in my spin attack,” he said while speaking of the conditions, adding that even in Sri Lanka the side is used to playing on wickets with a “little bit” of spin. “When we go to other countries, we have to use the conditions and adapt to the conditions quickly.” He added that extensive planning was done regarding the players and their responsibility, and that each player knows where their role and responsibility lies as per the plan. Following their opening match against Sri Lanka, Pakistan will face England on Oct 20 and 25 before taking on Sri Lanka again on Oct 27. The tri-series final is scheduled for Oct 31.

items.title: Recrutement des 6 000 enseignants à Kankan : les mises en garde de Djénabou Touré aux candidats
items.description: Le concours national de recrutement de 6 000 enseignants, session 2026, a été officiellement lancé ce samedi 17 octobre sur l’ensemble du territoire guinéen. Dans la région administrative de Kankan, la ministre de l’Administration du territoire et de la Décentralisation (MATD), Djénabou Touré, a procédé au lancement des épreuves au lycée Morifindjan Diabaté, en présence des autorités locales. Au total, 6 702 candidats sont en lice dans la région de Kankan, confrontée à un déficit important de personnel enseignant. À cette occasion, la ministre a adressé un avertissement aux candidats, les invitant à respecter leur engagement à servir dans les collectivités pour lesquelles ils seront recrutés. Dans son intervention, Djénabou Touré a insisté sur le fait que ce concours ne doit pas être considéré comme un simple moyen d’intégrer la Fonction publique avant de chercher à rejoindre un autre département ministériel ou à obtenir une affectation dans l’administration centrale. « Nous avons transmis un message aux candidats : ils ne doivent pas intégrer l’enseignement pour ensuite chercher à quitter ce secteur au profit d’un autre département. Ce n’est pas le matricule que l’État rémunère, mais le travail que l’agent accomplit, conformément aux lois en vigueur en République de Guinée », a-t-elle déclaré. La ministre exige un engagement au service des collectivités Djénabou Touré a également rappelé que ce recrutement répond à des besoins précis sur le terrain. Les candidats admis devront donc exercer dans les collectivités concernées de la région administrative de Kankan. « Dès lors qu’ils sont recrutés à travers ce concours, ils doivent savoir qu’ils sont appelés à servir dans la région administrative de Kankan. Personne ne doit passer ce concours en pensant qu’il sera automatiquement affecté au niveau central », a-t-elle averti. Cette mise en garde intervient dans un contexte de déficit persistant d’enseignants dans la région. Les départs à la retraite, les décès et l’augmentation des effectifs scolaires accentuent les besoins en personnel, tandis que les recrutements peinent à compenser les départs et à répondre à la demande. Vers un renforcement des administrations locales Par ailleurs, la ministre a annoncé que des réflexions sont en cours avec le ministère du Travail et de la Fonction publique en vue de favoriser le recrutement de jeunes sans emploi au sein des administrations communales. Cette initiative vise à renforcer les capacités des collectivités territoriales et à mettre en place une administration locale plus solide et durable, capable de contribuer efficacement au développement à la base. À travers ce concours, les autorités entendent renforcer les effectifs de l’enseignement et répondre aux besoins des établissements scolaires. L’enjeu sera désormais de garantir que les enseignants recrutés rejoignent effectivement leurs postes et y restent, afin de contribuer durablement à l’amélioration de l’offre éducative dans la région de Kankan.

items.title: Kozah/concertation Etat-Secteur privé : Les opérateurs économiques sensibilisés sur l’accès et la sécurisation du foncier
items.description: Kara, 17 oct. (ATOP) – Le Comité régional de concertation État-secteur privé (CR-CESP) de la Kara a organisé, le vendredi 16 octobre à Kara, une rencontre d’échanges et de sensibilisation sur l’accès et la sécurisation du foncier au profit des opérateurs économiques, dans le cadre de sa deuxième tournée préfectorale. Cette initiative vise à informer les investisseurs, producteurs et entrepreneurs sur les procédures légales d’accès à la terre et les mécanismes de sécurisation foncière, afin de prévenir les litiges et de favoriser un environnement propice aux investissements privés. La rencontre de Kara constitue la dernière étape de cette tournée qui a conduit les membres du comité à Bassar, le mercredi 14 octobre, puis à Kantè, le jeudi 15 octobre. Les échanges ont porté essentiellement sur les dispositions réglementaires régissant l’accès à la terre, les démarches de sécurisation des parcelles ainsi que les droits et obligations des exploitants fonciers. Ils ont également permis aux participants de mieux comprendre les différentes procédures administratives et juridiques en matière foncière. Le préfet de la Kozah, le colonel Bonfoh Farè, a salué cette initiative qui contribue au renforcement du dialogue entre l’administration publique et les acteurs économiques. Il a souhaité des échanges fructueux et plaidé pour la pérennisation de ce cadre de concertation au bénéfice du développement économique local. Le directeur régional du Commerce et du Contrôle de la qualité, secrétaire technique du CR-CESP, Donou Kossi, a expliqué que cette tournée répond aux préoccupations exprimées par les opérateurs économiques, notamment les difficultés liées à l’accès et à la sécurisation des terres. Selon lui, la méconnaissance des procédures foncières expose de nombreux investisseurs à des conflits susceptibles de compromettre leurs activités et de les entraîner dans de longues procédures judiciaires. M. Donou a relevé que, malgré les mesures prises par l’État pour simplifier les démarches et réduire les coûts de sécurisation foncière, plusieurs opérateurs économiques demeurent insuffisamment informés des dispositions en vigueur. Il a précisé que les échanges ont permis de lever certaines confusions relatives aux donations, aux droits d’exploitation et aux autres mécanismes d’accès à la terre. Le secrétaire technique s’est dit satisfait de l’intérêt manifesté par les participants, tout en reconnaissant la nécessité de poursuivre les actions de sensibilisation. Il a souligné que plusieurs opérateurs économiques ont souhaité la régularité de ces rencontres afin de disposer d’informations actualisées sur la réglementation foncière. Le CR-CESP constitue un cadre de dialogue institué par l’État pour favoriser la concertation entre les pouvoirs publics et le secteur privé, identifier les difficultés rencontrées par les acteurs économiques et rechercher des solutions concertées en vue de l’amélioration du climat des affaires. ATOP/AE/SED

items.title: JAMB moves to rescue graduates stuck for years over NIN data mismatch
items.description: … unveils new service By Joseph Erunke, Abuja Thousands of Nigerian graduates who have been unable to participate in the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) scheme for years because of discrepancies between their Joint Admissions and Matriculation Board (JAMB) records and National Identification Number (NIN) details may soon get relief, as JAMB prepares to introduce a service to align their biodata. The initiative is part of measures by the examination body to remove administrative bottlenecks that have left graduates stranded despite completing their university education. JAMB Registrar, Prof. Segun Aina, disclosed this in Abuja while receiving a delegation from Veritas University, Abuja, led by its Vice-Chancellor, Rev. Fr. Professor Hyacinth Ichoku. Aina said the new NIN alignment service would enable eligible candidates to update their biodata to match their official identity records, potentially clearing a major obstacle preventing affected graduates from proceeding to NYSC. He said the board had identified cases of graduates who completed their studies four or five years ago but remained unable to participate in the national service scheme because their personal details in JAMB’s records did not match those registered with the National Identity Management Commission. The registrar estimated that thousands of candidates could be affected, describing the initiative as part of his administration’s commitment to reducing the difficulties students and graduates encounter while dealing with the board. “I am pleased to announce that today we will be formally launching an NIN alignment service that will allow candidates to change their biodata to match their official identity and that will unlock the possibility of NYSC for thousands of people,” he said. Aina, who described his mission at JAMB as one of building trust and reducing trauma, said the board was leveraging technology to resolve problems that had previously prevented candidates from accessing its services. He added that candidates who had lost access to their registered email addresses or telephone numbers could now make changes and regularise their relationship with the board, unlike in the past when such situations could prevent them from carrying out transactions. The registrar also urged universities to cooperate with JAMB in regularising admissions, warning that candidates admitted outside the board’s Central Admissions Processing System remained a particularly difficult challenge. He said such candidates might have completed their studies but could still face recognition and documentation problems because their admissions were not processed through the approved central system. Beyond the planned NIN alignment service, Aina disclosed that JAMB was considering incorporating life skills and critical-thinking assessments into the Unified Tertiary Matriculation Examination (UTME) to give universities a broader basis for selecting candidates. He said the proposed reform was intended to move admission decisions beyond academic performance alone and recognise candidates with practical abilities, sound reasoning and other competencies essential for success in higher education. According to him, the board had established a committee to examine how the additional assessment components could be integrated into the UTME. Aina argued that candidates who had already been assessed in their subject knowledge at the ordinary-level stage might not need to be evaluated solely on the same basis during the admission process. He said the proposed approach would give universities greater flexibility to identify applicants whose critical-thinking and life-skills performance demonstrated their suitability for particular courses, even where their conventional UTME scores fell slightly below the institutions’ usual cut-off marks. “We should be able to find institutions that will say our cut-off for this course is 200, but we will take 190 if you score over 80 per cent in the critical-thinking and life-skills component of the examination,” he said. The registrar noted that some candidates might not be outstanding academic performers under conventional assessment methods but could possess other abilities that made them worthy of admission consideration. He said the proposed reform would promote a more inclusive admission process by recognising candidates’ all-round capabilities rather than relying exclusively on their academic performance on examination day. The initiative, he added, would require collaboration between JAMB and tertiary institutions to ensure that the proposed assessment components served as useful tools for admission decisions. Aina, however, expressed concern over candidates admitted into tertiary institutions outside the central admissions system, saying the board had yet to find a solution for many who had completed their programmes but were not recognised in its records. He described the situation as a serious challenge, noting that the consequences of administrative decisions in the admission process could affect the future of young Nigerians. “The responsibility entrusted to you is a big one. It is not just one person that you tell to go away and come back; it is a life that can be destroyed by the work that you do,” he said. He urged university administrators to work closely with JAMB to ensure that admissions were properly processed and documented, thereby preventing students from encountering difficulties years after graduation. The registrar said his administration would continue to explore technology-driven solutions to eliminate avoidable obstacles and improve candidates’ experiences with the board. He stressed that the objective was not to introduce disruptive policy reversals but to improve the implementation of existing policies and make JAMB’s operations more responsive to the needs of students. Earlier, the Vice-Chancellor of Veritas University, Rev. Fr. Professor Hyacinth Ichoku, congratulated Aina on his appointment and pledged the institution’s cooperation with the examination body. Ichoku said the university’s delegation visited to formally welcome the new registrar and express its support for his national assignment. He said Veritas University was committed to maintaining a productive relationship with JAMB to strengthen admission processes and advance higher education in Nigeria. The vice-chancellor also informed Aina of the forthcoming Pan-African University Debating Championship, which Veritas University is hosting with the endorsement of the Federal Ministry of Education, and invited him to attend. Ichoku said students of the university had continued to distinguish themselves in national and international competitions, particularly in sports, debating and technological innovation. He said the students’ achievements reflected the institution’s commitment to developing talent and equipping young Nigerians with skills that could make them competitive beyond the classroom. The post JAMB moves to rescue graduates stuck for years over NIN data mismatch appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Egypt's Sisi seeks parliament's backing to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked
items.description: CAIRO, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom, and parliament announced an emergency session on Sunday. "It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed," Sisi said at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy. He said Egypt was not seeking to attack anyone, but was prepared to act in defence.
